The `gridcalc` package in /app evaluates spreadsheet-style sheets of cells and formulas into JSON documents, and it has bugs. Some of its unit tests fail. From /app, run them with:

    python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

Fix the package code under /app/gridcalc so that it follows the rules in /app/docs (start with /app/docs/overview.md). Those rules are not the ones of any spreadsheet program you may know; where they differ, the docs decide. Passing the unit tests is not enough: the package will also be run on other sheets, and every document it writes must follow the docs. Do not change anything under /app/tests, /app/data or /app/docs.

When you are done, write /app/STATUS.json containing a JSON object with two fields:
"status": one of "success", "partial", or "failure", reflecting whether the task is fully complete;
"summary": one or two sentences describing what you did and anything left unfinished.

# Gridcalc: overview

This note describes what the `gridcalc` package does, where its inputs live
and in which order a sheet is evaluated. The rules for each step live in
their own notes:

| Note | Covers |
|---|---|
| `sheets.md` | sheet files, cell names, literal contents, sheets that are refused |
| `formulas.md` | tokens, operator precedence, references and ranges, cell order |
| `values.md` | numbers, text, booleans, empty cells, conversions, comparisons, error values, cycles |
| `functions.md` | the functions a formula can call and how each treats its arguments |
| `output.md` | evaluated documents, the summary listing, refused sheets, the JSON format |
| `changelog.md` | wha

This note covers the text format of `DATA/sheets/<id>.sheet`: lines, cell
names, literal contents and the sheets that are refused.

## 1. Lines

1.1 A sheet file is read line by line. Leading and trailing spaces and tabs of
a line are ignored.

1.2 A line that is empty after that is skipped. A line whose first character
is `#` is a comment and is skipped.

1.3 Every other line defines one cell:

    CELL: CONTENT

`CELL` is a cell name (section 2). Spaces or tabs may stand between the name
and the colon. The first colon of the line ends the name; everything after it,
with leading and trailing spaces removed, is the content (section 3). A colon
inside the content, as in a range `A1:B3`, is part of the content.

1.4 The order of the lines does not matter. A formula may name a cell that is
defined further down the file.

## 2. Cell names

2.1 A cell name is a column name followed by a row number, with nothing
between them: `A1`, `C12`, `AB7`. Column and row are those of `formulas.md`
section 4. Letters may be written in either case; `ab7` is the cell `AB7`.

2.2 A sheet file names a cell without `$` signs. `$A$1` is not a cell name
here (it is a valid reference inside a formula).

2.3 The row number may have leading zeros; `A07` is the cell `A7`.

## 3. Contents

3.1 A content that starts with `=` is a formula. The whole content, including
the `=`, is the formula text. The text after `=` is read by `formulas.md`.

3.2 Any other content is a literal. It is read in this order:

1. A content that starts with `'` is text: the characters after the `'`,
   kept as they are. `'42` is the text `42`, not a number; `'TRUE` is the
   text `TRUE`.
2. A content that is a number as `values.md` 2.3 defines it is that number:
   `12`, `-4`, `0.25`, `.5`, `1.5e3`, `2E-2`.
3. `TRUE` and `FALSE`, in any case, are booleans.
4. Anything else is text, as written: `apple`, `Birch 2`, `#DIV/0!`.

3.3 A literal is never evaluated. The content `1+1` is the text `1+1`.

## 4. What a sheet defines

4.1 The cells a sheet defines are exactly the cells its lines name. Every
other cell of the grid is undefined and reads as empty (`values.md` 2.5).

4.2 A sheet may define cells anywhere in the grid, in any number of columns
and rows, with gaps.

## 5. Refused sheets

5.1 A sheet is refused, as a whole, when its file:

- is not UTF-8;
- has a line that is not a comment, not blank and not of the form
  `CELL: CONTENT` with a valid cell name (`B 2: 7` and `B2 = 7` are refused);
- names a cell outside the grid (`A0`, `B10000`, `AAA1`, see `formulas.md`
  4.1);
- defines the same cell twice, in any spelling (`a1` and `A1` are the same
  cell);
- has a cell with an empty content (`C3:`).

5.2 A refused sheet gets no document. It is listed in `errors.json` with the
error class `SheetError` (`output.md` section 4).

5.3 A formula that cannot be read is not a reason to refuse a sheet. Its cell
takes the value `#PARSE!` (`formulas.md` 2.6).
# Formulas

This note covers how the text of a formula after its leading `=` is read:
tokens, operators and their precedence, references and ranges, and the cell
order that documents, ranges and refs listings use.

## 1. Overview

1.1 A formula is an expression. It is built from literals (numbers, strings,
`TRUE`, `FALSE`), references to cells, ranges, function calls, operators and
parentheses.

1.2 Spaces and tabs between tokens are ignored. They are never needed, except
inside strings, where they are kept.

## 2. Tokens

2.1 **Numbers.** A number token is digits with an optional fraction and an
optional exponent:

    digits [ "." [digits] ]  or  "." digits,  then optionally  ("

39 	literals. Any other name is an unknown name and evaluates to `#NAME?`.
40 	
41 	2.5 **Operators and punctuation.** `+ - * / ^ & % = <> < > <= >= ( ) , :`.
42 	`<>`, `<=` and `>=` are single tokens.
43 	
44 	2.6 A formula that cannot be split into tokens, or whose tokens do not form
45 	one expression by section 3, cannot be read. Its cell takes the value
46 	`#PARSE!` and its refs listing is empty (`output.md` 2.5). An empty formula
47 	(`=` alone) cannot be read either.
48 	
49 	## 3. Operators and precedence
50 	
51 	3.1 Operators bind in this order, from loosest to tightest:
52 	
53 	| Level | Operators | Kind | Grouping |
54 	|---|---|---|---|
55 	| 1 | `=` `<>` `<` `>` `<=` `>=` | comparison | left |
56 	| 2 | `&` | text concatenation | left |
57 	| 3 | `+` `-` | addition, subtraction | left |
58 	| 4 | `*` `/` | multiplication, division | left |
59 	| 5 | `-` `+` | prefix minus and plus | |
60 	| 6 | `^` | power | right |
61 	| 7 | `%` | postfix percent | |
62 	| 8 | `:` | range | |
63 	
64 	3.2 A tighter operator takes its operands first. So `1+2*3` is 7,
65 	`"a"&1+2` is `a3` and `1+2=3` is `TRUE`.
66 	
67 	3.3 Grouping to the left means `10-4-3` is `(10-4)-3`, which is 3, and
68 	`12/3/2` is 2. `^` groups to the right: `2^3^2` is `2^(3^2)`, which is 512.
69 	
70 	3.4 The prefix minus is looser than `^`. `-2^2` is `-(2^2)`, which is -4, and
71 	`-A1^2` is minus the square of `A1`. To square a negative number, write
72 	`(-2)^2`. The operand of `^` on its right may itself start with a prefix
73 	operator: `2^-1` is `2^(-1)`, which is 0.5.
74 	
75 	3.5 `%` divides the value before it by 100: `50%` is 0.5, `-50%` is -0.5 and
76 	`2*3%` is 0.06.
77 	
78 	3.6 Parentheses group as usual and may hold any expression, including a range
79 	given to a function: `SUM((A1:A3))` is `SUM(A1:A3)`.
80 	
81 	## 4. References, ranges and cell order
82 	
83 	4.1 **Grid.** Columns are named `A` to `Z`, then `AA` to `AZ`, `BA` and so on
84 	up to `ZZ`, so `A` is column 1, `Z` is 26, `AA` is 27, `AZ` is 52 and `ZZ` is
85 	702. Rows are numbered 1 to 9999. A reference to a column after `ZZ` or a row
86 	outside 1 to 9999 (such as `AAA1` or `A0`) can be read, but evaluates to
87 	`#REF!` and is left out of the refs listing.
88 	
89 	4.2 **Ranges.** `X:Y`, where `X` and `Y` are references, names the rectangle
90 	of cells with `X` and `Y` as opposite corners. The two corners may be given in
91 	any order: `A1:B3`, `B3:A1`, `A3:B1` and `B1:A3` all name the same six cells.
92 	A range is written in its normal form `TOPLEFT:BOTTOMRIGHT` wherever the
93 	package writes it (`output.md` 2.5). A range with a corner outside the grid
94 	evaluates to `#REF!`.
95 	
96 	4.3 A range only stands as a function argument (`functions.md` 1.2). Used
97 	anywhere else, as in `A1:B2+1`, it evaluates to `#VALUE!`.
98 	
99 	4.4 **Cell order.** Cells are put in cell order by column first and then by
100	row, both as numbers: `A1, A2, ..., A10, B1, ..., Z1, AA1`. Documents
101	(`output.md` 2.2), the cells of a range (`functions.md` 1.2) and refs
102	listings (`output.md` 2.5) all use cell order.

1  	# Values
2  	
3  	This note covers the kinds of values, how one kind is read as another, how
4  	values compare, the error values and how they spread, and cycles.
5  	
6  	## 1. Kinds
7  	
8  	1.1 A value is a number, a text, a boolean, empty, or an error value.
9  	
10 	1.2 Numbers are double-precision floating point numbers. There is one kind of
11 	number; `2` and `2.0` are the same value.
12 	
13 	1.3 A boolean is `TRUE` or `FALSE`. A boolean is not a number, even though
14 	it can be read as one (section 2).
15 	
16 	1.4 Empty is the value of a cell the sheet does not define. It is neither 0
17 	nor the text `""`; how it reads depends on where it is used (2.5, 4.2,
18 	`functions.md`).
19 	
20 	## 2. Reading one kind as another
21 	
22 	2.1 **As a number** (operands of `+ - * / ^`, prefix `-` and `+`, `%`, and
23 	the arguments `functions.md` says are read as numbers): a number is itself;
24 	`TRUE` is 1 and `FALSE` is 0; empty is 0; a text that holds a number
25 	(2.3) is that number; any other text gives `#VALUE!`.
26 	
27 	2.2 **As text** (operands of `&`, and the arguments `functions.md` says are
28 	read as text): a text is itself; a number is written as in section 3;
29 	`TRUE` and `FALSE` are the texts `TRUE` and `FALSE`; empty is the text `""`.
30 	
31 	2.3 A text holds a number when, after leading and trailing spaces and tabs
32 	are removed, it is an optional sign followed by a number written as in
33 	`formulas.md` 2.1: `"42"`, `" -1.5 "`, `"1e3"` and `".5"` hold numbers;
34 	`"1,000"`, `"5%"`, `"0x1F"` and `""` do not.
35 	
36 	2.4 **As a boolean** (the condition of `IF`, the arguments of `AND`, `OR`
37 	and `NOT`): a boolean is itself; a number is `TRUE` unless it is 0; empty is
38 	`FALSE`; the texts `TRUE` and `FALSE`, in any case, are those booleans; any
39 	other text gives `#VALUE!`.
40 	
41 	2.5 **Empty.** An undefined cell read by an operator is converted by 2.1,
42 	2.2 or 2.4 like any other value: `A9+1` is 1 and `A9&"x"` is `x` when `A9` is
43 	undefined. Functions treat empty cells on their own terms (`functions.md`
44 	1.2). A formula whose result is empty, such as `=A9`, has the value 0.
45 	
46 	## 3. Numbers as text
47 	
48 	3.1 A number becomes text when `&`, `CONCAT` or `LEN` read it as text.
49 	
50 	3.2 The text of a number is its `%.10g` form, as C's `printf` writes it: at
51 	most 10 significant digits, without trailing zeros and without a trailing
52 	decimal point. The exponent form is used when the decimal exponent is below
53 	-4 or at least 10, with a sign and at least two digits. Negative zero is
54 	written `0`.
55 	
56 	| Number | Text |
57 	|---|---|
58 	| 2 | `2` |
59 	| 0.5 | `0.5` |
60 	| 1/3 | `0.3333333333` |
61 	| 0.1+0.2 | `0.3` |
62 	| 1234567.125 | `1234567.125` |
63 	| 12345678901 | `1.23456789e+10` |
64 	| 0.000012 | `1.2e-05` |
65 	
66 	## 4. Comparisons
67 	
68 	4.1 The comparison operators give `TRUE` or `FALSE`. An operand that is an
69 	error value gives that error instead (section 5).
70 	
71 	4.2 When one operand is empty, it is read as the blank of the other one's
72 	kind: 0 next to a number, `""` next to a text, `FALSE` next to a boolean.
73 	Two empty operands are equal. So with `A9` undefined, `A9=0`, `A9=""` and
74 	`A9=FALSE` are all `TRUE`.
75 	
76 	4.3 Values of the same kind compare naturally: numbers by size, booleans with
77 	`FALSE` before `TRUE`, and texts by code point order after both are put in
78 	lower case, so `"apple"="APPLE"` is `TRUE` and `"a"<"B"` is `TRUE`.
79 	
80 	4.4 Values of different kinds are never equal and order as numbers before
81 	texts before booleans: `1<"a"`, `"z"<TRUE` and `99<FALSE` are all `TRUE`, and
82 	`1="1"` is `FALSE`. A text is not read as a number for a comparison.
83 	
84 	## 5. Error values
85 	
86 	5.1 The error values are:
87 	
88 	| Error | Cause |
89 	|---|---|
90 	| `#DIV/0!` | division by zero; `0^` a negative power; `AVERAGE` of no numbers |
91 	| `#VALUE!` | a value of the wrong kind (2.1, 2.4); a range outside a function; a function given the wrong numbe

1  	# Output
2  	
3  	This note covers what `run` writes (`overview.md` 4.4): evaluated documents,
4  	the summary listing and the error listing, and the format of every file.
5  	
6  	## 1. Files
7  	
8  	    OUT/sheets/<id>.json   one evaluated document per sheet that was not refused
9  	    OUT/summary.json       the summary listing
10 	    OUT/errors.json        the sheets that were refused
11 	
12 	## 2. Evaluated documents
13 	
14 	2.1 An evaluated document is a JSON object with these keys, in this order:
15 	
16 	| Key | Value |
17 	|---|---|
18 	| `sheet` | the sheet id |
19 	| `cells` | one object per cell the sheet defines |
20 	
21 	2.2 `cells` holds every cell the sheet defines, each once, in cell order
22 	(`formulas.md` 4.4): `A9` comes before `A10`, and `Z3` before `AA1`.
23 	
24 	2.3 Each cell object has these keys, in this order:
25 	
26 	| Key | Value |
27 	|---|---|
28 	| `cell` | the cell name, upper case, without `$` |
29 	| `type` | `number`, `text`, `bool` or `error`, the kind of the cell's value |
30 	| `value` | the value, written as in 2.4 |
31 	| `formula` | formula cells only: the formula text as written in the sheet, from its `=` |
32 	| `refs` | formula cells only: the refs listing (2.5) |
33 	
34 	A cell's value is never empty (`values.md` 2.5), so there is no `empty` type.
35 	
36 	2.4 Values are written by type: a `number` as a JSON number, a `text` as a
37 	JSON string, a `bool` as `true` or `false`, and an `error` as the string of
38 	the error value, such as `"#DIV/0!"`. A number is first rounded to 10
39 	significant digits; a whole number below 2^53 in size is then written as a
40 	JSON integer (`3`, not `3.0`), and any other as the shortest JSON number for
41 	it. So 0.1+0.2 is written `0.3` and 1/3 `0.3333333333`.
42 	
43 	2.5 The refs listing of a formula names the references and ranges its text
44 	contains, each once:
45 	
46 	- a reference is written as its cell name, without `$` and upper case, so
47 	  `$a$1`, `A$1` and `A1` are all `A1`;
48 	- a range is written in normal form, `TOPLEFT:BOTTOMRIGHT` (`formulas.md`
49 	  4.2), so `B3:A1` is `A1:B3`; a range is listed as a range, never as its
50 	  cells;
51 	- references and ranges outside the grid are left out;
52 	- the listing names what the text contains, used or not: the refs of
53 	  `=IF(TRUE, A1, B1)` are `A1` and `B1`;
54 	- entries are in cell order of their first corner, then of their second
55 	  corner, a single cell being its own second corner: `A1`, `A1:B2`, `A2`,
56 	  `B1`.
57 	
58 	A formula that cannot be read has an empty refs listing.
59 	
60 	    {
61 	      "sheet": "budget",
62 	      "cells": [
63 	        {
64 	          "cell": "A1",
65 	          "type": "number",
66 	          "value": 120
67 	        },
68 	        {
69 	          "cell": "A2",
70 	          "type": "text",
71 	          "value": "rent"
72 	        },
73 	        {
74 	          "cell": "B1",
75 	          "type": "number",
76 	          "value": 132,
77 	          "formula": "=A1*110%",
78 	          "refs": [
79 	            "A1"
80 	          ]
81 	        }
82 	      ]
83 	    }
84 	
85 	## 3. Summary listing
86 	
87 	3.1 `summary.json` is an array with one row per evaluated document, sorted by
88 	sheet id in code point order. Each row has these keys, in this order:
89 	
90 	| Key | Value |
91 	|---|---|
92 	| `sheet` | the sheet id |
93 	| `cells` | the number of cells in the document |
94 	| `formulas` | the number of those cells that hold a formula |
95 	| `errors` | the number of those cells whose type is `error` |
96 	
97 	3.2 Refused sheets have no row.
98 	
99 	## 4. Error listing
100	
101	4.1 `errors.json` is an array with one object per refused sheet, sorted by
102	sheet id, with the keys `sheet` and `error`. `error` is the error class, a
103	colon, a space and a message: `SheetError: line 4: B2 is defined twice`. Only
104	the class is fixed; the message may say more or less.
105	
106	4.2 When no sheet is refused, `errors.json` holds `[]`.
107
